items.text: SEASON 7 · EPISODE 9 · DRAFT  Governance · Maya, Henrik, Luis, Mara and Adaeze · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  The board wants Standard v3 in twenty pages. Every region has sent its wish list. The exception register hasn’t been read in a year.  ⚑ RV-150: each clause has an owner. RV-151: counts illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Standard v3
items.stakes: The board wants a new standard in twenty pages. Every region wants its wishes in it. The register of exceptions hasn't been read in a year.
items.reward: A standard that's short because it's clear — and a register that tells the truth.

objectives.text: Decide what happens to expired exceptions

items.rumor: Twenty pages. Forty sites. Whose wishes?

items.alt: The executive floor; Henrik holds the thick v2 binder bristling with regional sticky notes; Maya across the table.

bubbles.text: Twenty pages. The board won't read more. And every region wants its wishes in.
Then every page has to be something a room can pass or fail.

items.caption: End of quarter: eleven weeks.

lines.text: Twenty pages. The board won't read more.

items.prompt: 10:00. How does v3 get to twenty pages?
items.happening: v2: 140 clauses; wish lists from every region.
items.risk: A short standard that no longer protects anyone.
timeout: The week goes to other fires.
Henrik's assistant starts cutting sections to hit twenty pages.

hints.text: Which clauses could a room pass or fail — and which are someone's taste?

options.label: Cut the longest sections until it fits
options.result: The longest were intelligibility guidance and accessibility. Gone.
options.fail: Length isn't the enemy; vagueness is.

options.label: Sort every clause — testable requirement, preference, regional variant — then write tests for the requirements and see how long it is
options.result: By Wednesday: 64 requirements, 60 preferences, 16 variants — and four outcomes v2 never required.
options.consequence: Know what you have before you cut.

options.label: Let each region write its own standard
options.result: Forty sites, three standards, no shared support.

options.label: Keep v2 and add a summary page
options.result: Twenty-one pages on top of eighty-eight.

items.title: Somebody's taste.
items.body: Sorted, v2 is 64 testable requirements, 60 preferences — a panel model, blue status lights, rack paint, a ‘premium feel’ — and 16 regional variants written as if they were global. And four outcomes appear nowhere: that people can understand each other (speech intelligibility), that a call starts in under a minute, that captions are available, that devices are administered through named accounts.
items.label: Test: how many requirements in v3 — and what did v2 never require?

items.alt: A standard sheet for v2: a bar of 140 clauses — 64 green requirements, 60 grey preferences, 16 teal variants; missing: intelligibility, join time, captions, named accounts; the register: 96 exceptions, 38 past their end dates.
items.caption: Forty-three percent taste.

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Henrik and Maya beside a board. A hundred and forty clauses. Cut it to twenty pages. Sixty of them are preferences — forty-three percent. The rest become tests a room can pass or fail. That's the standard. Forty-three percent of my standard is somebody's taste. Wonderful. And the exceptions?

items.title: The register nobody reads.
items.body: The exception register holds 96 entries. 38 have passed their end dates — 40% of the register quietly turned from design into drift. One of them is EX-017: Valmera's boardroom loop, recorded as ‘temporary’ four years ago. It was never temporary. It's the law.
items.label: Test: how much of the register has expired — and what is EX-017 really?

items.prompt: Thursday. What happens to the 38 expired exceptions?
unknown: Which of the 38 are still needed
items.risk: Drift disguised as design — or law flagged as drift.

hints.text: Who can say whether each exception still has a reason?

options.label: Renew them all for another year
options.result: Thirty-eight unexamined differences, stamped as design again.
options.fail: An exception is a decision, not a habit.

options.label: Each goes back to its owner: fold it into v3 as a variant, fix it as drift with a date, or renew it with a reason — the change board reviews the register every quarter, and the scanner treats an expired exception as drift
options.result: EX-017 becomes a permanent Valmera variant; 21 become drift tickets with dates; 16 are renewed with reasons.
options.consequence: Owners decide; the register tells the truth.

options.label: Delete every expired exception
options.result: The scanner flags Valmera's loop — a legal requirement — as drift the next morning.
options.fail: Some expired entries are records wrongly kept.

options.label: Leave the register alone — v3 is the priority
options.result: v3 launches on a register that's 40% fiction.
options.consequence: A standard with a lying appendix.

items.title: One screw thread
items.body: In 1841 the engineer Joseph Whitworth proposed that Britain's workshops use one screw thread — a fixed angle and a fixed number of threads per inch for each diameter — instead of every maker's own. It spread because it described what a thread must be, not whose machine had to cut it. The best standards still work that way.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #70 · AVERY'S LENS  Write requirements people can test  A rule that can't pass or fail is a preference. Say what the room must achieve, how it will be checked, and who owns the clause.  Standard v2 required a panel model and blue lights, and never required that people in the room could understand each other.

items.alt: The standard sheet for v3: a bar of 80 testable requirements — 64 kept, 16 added (intelligibility, join time, captions, named accounts); preferences moved to guidance and variants to approved annexes; every exception owned and dated; a change board.
items.caption: Shorter, and stricter.

items.prompt: Why do we need a change board? Can't you just decide what's in it?

options.label: “I could — and then it's my standard, and it leaves when I do. The board makes it Corvane's: the people whose rooms, laws and risks it holds.”
“Accessibility and security own their clauses. They need a seat.”

items.title: TP-7 (blue bezel)
items.body: Standard v2, clause 4.7: ‘Touch panel: TP-7 with blue bezel.’ Added in 2020, the margin note says, ‘per CEO preference’. The CEO left in 2021.

items.prompt: Friday. Who owns the standard from now on?
items.risk: A standard that decays the day it ships.
timeout: v3 ships with no owner named.
By spring, clauses are being added by email.

hints.text: Who would still keep it true if you left?

options.label: Maya approves every change herself
options.result: Fast — until Maya is on holiday, or leaves.

options.label: A change board — the regional leads, security, accessibility and the standard's owner — releases a version twice a year; every clause has an owner and a test
options.result: The first board meets Thursday; Mara and the accessibility lead each take their clauses.
options.consequence: The standard belongs to the people whose rooms, laws and risks it holds.

options.label: Henrik approves every change
options.result: Henrik: “I don't want to choose touch panels.”

options.label: No versions — edit it whenever
options.result: Nobody knows which rules a room was built to.
options.consequence: A standard that moves under you.

items.alt: After the board meeting: Henrik holding a slim v3 document; Luis with a single page titled VALMERA VARIANT · APPROVED.

bubbles.text: Twenty-two pages. The board read all of them.
And my loop is law again, not an exception.

items.title: temporary
items.body: Exception EX-017: ‘Valmera boardrooms — loop on output 1. Temporary. Review by last June.’ Nobody reviewed it; the law hasn't changed. It was never temporary.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A requirement states an outcome and its test; a preference names a product or a taste — it belongs in guidance. Standards get short by being clear, not by deleting accessibility or security. The exception register is half the standard: every entry owned, reasoned and dated, reviewed by a change board — and an expired exception is drift until its owner says otherwise.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Pick a rule you work under. Could you test whether you’re meeting it — or is it somebody’s taste?
